paper_metadata.title: Quantum support vector data description for anomaly detection

summary: The paper proposes Quantum Support Vector Data Description (QSVDD), a QCNN-based variational quantum anomaly detection model using 8 qubits and 75 trainable parameters. On MNIST it achieves mean AUC 83.13±2.15 compared to 70.54 (QAE) and 70.32 (DSVDD), and on Fashion‑MNIST 80.59±2.28 compared to 76.69 and 76.05 respectively, evaluated across 10 anomaly-detection tasks with ~6000 training samples each using PennyLane simulation.

experiments.description: Quantum support vector data description (QSVDD) anomaly detection on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST using a shallow variational quantum circuit with QCNN ansatz, compared against quantum autoencoder and classical deep SVDD baselines.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Support Vector Data Description (QSVDD) with QCNN ansatz
algorithm.convergence_criteria: minimize QSVDD loss; no explicit stopping criterion reported
algorithm.parameter_initialization: parameters initialized randomly from a standard normal distribution

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Classical images resized to 16x16 and amplitude-encoded into an 8-qubit state; each class treated as the normal class in one-class anomaly detection
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize the squared distance between encoded data representations and hypersphere center in latent space: L_Q(θ)=Σ_i ||d(x_i,θ)-c||^2
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: One-class hypersphere objective; anomalies are points outside the learned hypersphere

problem_instance.description: One-class anomaly detection on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, with each class in turn treated as the normal class

dataset_specification.description: 10 classes; 10 independent anomaly-detection tasks per dataset; each task uses one class as normal

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Images resized from 28x28 to 16x16 using bilinear interpolation for amplitude encoding
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Five random initializations per task; AUC computed for each task; results averaged over 10 tasks and 5 repetitions

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Amplitude encoding after bilinear image resizing; latent-space dimension selected by validation over measured Pauli observables
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: AUC evaluation; hypersphere center and radius used for anomaly scoring

results.unit: samples per task (training normal samples, approx.)

speedup_claims.factor: O(log n) circuit depth and O(log n) parameters for QCNN; compared with QAE scaling as O(n) parameters and O(n^2) depth
speedup_claims.conditions: as number of input qubits increases; QCNN ansatz used in QSVDD
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a scaling claim from the paper, not an empirical runtime benchmark.

speedup_claims.factor: doubly exponential reduction in number of parameters and circuit depth relative to input feature dimension when amplitude encoding is fully utilized
speedup_claims.conditions: if the exponentially large quantum state space is fully utilized
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper frames this as a potential advantage, not a measured speedup.

speedup_claims.factor: higher AUC than QAE and DSVDD on MNIST; higher AUC on 7/10 Fashion-MNIST tasks
speedup_claims.conditions: same training conditions, 8 input qubits, latent dimension 9, 5 random initializations, 10 AD tasks per dataset
speedup_claims.caveats: This is performance superiority, not computational speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Circuit depth and parameter count grow logarithmically with number of input qubits for QCNN; with amplitude encoding this implies doubly exponential reduction in parameters relative to input dimension
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: DSVDD and QAE baselines discussed qualitatively; no explicit asymptotic classical complexity for the full anomaly-detection task reported

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Unknown; experiments only simulate 8 qubits with amplitude encoding and QCNN ansatz
limiting_factors: Experiments only performed on noiseless simulator (PennyLane)
Amplitude encoding requires expensive state preparation that scales poorly with classical data size
No runtime comparison with classical algorithms
Improvement measured only in classification AUC on small benchmarks

notes: Hardware is not tied to a named QPU; PennyLane simulation is explicitly stated.
QCNN depth is described as O(log n) rather than a fixed numeric depth.
Classical baselines (QAE, DSVDD) are not separate experiments per instructions.
Authors emphasize improved anomaly-detection accuracy compared with QAE and DSVDD, but do not demonstrate computational speedup.
Scaling discussion (logarithmic circuit depth/parameters) refers to QCNN architecture properties rather than a proven quantum advantage.
